7FFN & output

The FFN expands, filters and shrinks each word’s vector, like looking up a “knowledge dictionary”; the final output scoring layer scores every word in the vocabulary, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

ⓘ Notes
The FFN expands, filters and shrinks each word’s vector, like looking up a “knowledge dictionary”; the final output scoring layer scores every word in the vocabulary, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

Why it’s designed this way: Attention only “moves” information; the real non-linear processing and knowledge storage happen mostly in the FFN.

Training means drilling the model on huge amounts of text with “guess the next word” exercises: after each guess the answer is checked, the more wrong it was the bigger the penalty (the loss), and then every parameter is nudged a tiny bit in the direction that lowers the penalty. Repeat billions to trillions of times.

Loss = −log(probability of the correct word): giving the right answer 70% means a loss of about 0.36; giving it only 10% means about 2.3.

Tap the cards below to see why the three training essentials are designed this way and why they work:

Massive data + next-word guessing

The training exercises: cut a passage from text and guess the word that follows.

Loss (cross-entropy)

A single number: how badly this question was guessed.

Backpropagation + gradient descent

Works out which way each parameter should move, then takes a small step.

Note: real training adjusts all parameters (thousands up to hundreds of billions of numbers in all kinds of tables); the scores only change as a result. To keep it intuitive, this demo pushes the scores directly. Also, during training every position in a sentence guesses its own next word at the same time (a “mask” stops it from peeking at the answer), so one sentence is many exercises at once.
Inside the Transformer block:
② Diagram

🧒 In plain words first

After the meeting, each word goes back to its desk to think: its list of numbers is first blown up into lots of little “detectors”, each recognising one pattern; a “switch” keeps lit only the detectors that found something; then the lit signals are added up and shrunk back to the original length. Pick a word below and follow it step by step (the numbers are an example).

Two big tables with a “filter switch” in between: first the vector is expanded into a longer list (typically about 4× as long), where each number acts like a “feature detector”; the switch keeps only the useful detectors on; the second table then gathers the active signals and compresses them back to the original length.

🧪 Mini demo Sample data: 3 input numbers → expanded to 12 → back to 3
Pick a word’s vector

① Input (3 numbers)

0.90-0.200.50

② Multiply by big table 1 → expand into 12 “detector” readings

0.88-0.58-0.16-0.100.99-0.170.25-0.920.93-0.11-0.220.32

③ Filter switch: negatives become 0, 5 detectors lit

0.880.000.000.000.990.000.250.000.930.000.000.32

④ Multiply by big table 2 → shrink back to 3 numbers (this step’s “increment”, added back to the original vector through the residual)

0.540.200.36
Why does it need a “filter switch”? Without it, two tables multiplied in a row are mathematically just one table, and no matter how many layers you stack you only get a “simple linear transformation”. With the switch the model can express complex “if … then …” patterns. Today smoother switches than ReLU are common (e.g. GELU, SwiGLU; SwiGLU also uses an extra table).
Many studies suggest that much of the “knowledge” a model memorizes (such as “Paris is the capital of France”) is stored mainly in these two big feed-forward tables.
Feed-forward networkEach word “digests and thinks” on its own, drawing on learned knowledge.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Attention is essentially “mixing everyone’s value cards in proportion” (for the content it’s a weighted average, basically linear), so it can only move and mix information. A part with a non-linear switch is needed to process the information into new features and express complex rules like “if … then …”; without non-linearity, stacking any number of layers equals just one layer.

✅ Why this works

Expanding and then compressing amounts to a very large “lookup + processing” unit: after expansion, thousands of detectors each recognize one pattern, and when one lights up it writes the matching information into the result. Many parameters, large capacity — it can remember a great many regularities.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Factual knowledge lives mainly in the feed-forward network” is an empirical observation from research (e.g. editing certain feed-forward parameters can change a fact the model remembers), not a rigorous proof; how knowledge is actually stored is still being researched.

Big table 1 (expand)Expands the vector into a longer list (typically about 4× as long).

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Expanding to a longer list (about 4×) amounts to preparing lots of “detectors”, each recognizing one pattern; the more detectors, the more patterns can be remembered and told apart.

✅ Why this works

Each detector’s reading = the dot product of the input vector with its row; the more aligned, the higher the reading, so “this word fits some pattern” gets detected.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A single detector often reacts to several unrelated patterns at once; it is not always “one detector, one concept”.

Filter switch (activation function)Decides which detectors are “on” and which are “off”.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Table multiplication is linear: two tables multiplied in a row still equal one table, and without non-linearity a hundred layers amount to just one. The switch introduces a “bend”, letting the model express “output only when a condition holds”.

✅ Why this works

With non-linearity, a stack of layers can express very complex rules; the switch also keeps most detectors “off” for a given word, so each word only calls up the small relevant part of the knowledge.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Which switch is best (ReLU / GELU / SwiGLU) was mainly settled by comparing experiments.

Big table 2 (compress)Gathers the active features and compresses them back to the original length.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Active detectors need to write “what I found” back into the word vector; each column of the second table is “what to write” for the corresponding detector.

✅ Why this works

After compressing back to the original length, the result is added to the original vector through the residual. The whole “expand–filter–compress” works like a giant “key → value” table: the rows of big table 1 act like “keys” (patterns to match) and the columns of big table 2 like “values” (information to write).

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Key–value memory” is a common interpretive lens in research, not a rigorous proof.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The residual is like sticking notes on the original draft: each layer only adds a small note, and the draft is always kept. So even after dozens of layers the original meaning is not lost, and during training the “how to fix it” signal can travel back along this straight road.

🔍 Go deeper (the full explanation)
Residual connection Tap for details

The result of each step doesn’t replace the original vector; it is added to the original vector.

Benefit: information doesn’t “get lost” across dozens of layers, and during training the adjustment signal can flow back to earlier layers along this “express lane”.

Residual connectionAdds the step’s result to the original vector instead of replacing it.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

In a very deep network, the training signal from the last layer back to the first passes through dozens of multiplications and can easily shrink away (vanishing gradients) or get distorted; and if every layer rewrote the whole vector, the original information would easily be lost.

✅ Why this works

Each layer only adds a small correction to the original vector, which leaves an “express lane”: gradients flow back to earlier layers almost unchanged and information isn’t lost. If a layer isn’t useful for now, it can just learn to “add 0” without breaking anything.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Normalisation is like setting everyone’s volume to about the same after each round of discussion, so nobody keeps getting louder or fades to a whisper. With the sizes of the numbers kept steady, the later steps and the training are much less likely to go wild.

🔍 Go deeper (the full explanation)
Normalization Tap for details

However big or small the numbers were, they are adjusted to “mean around 0, similar spread”.

The demo above is the classic LayerNorm; most current LLMs use RMSNorm, which skips the mean and only evens out the overall size: cheaper, and about as good.

NormalizationBrings a list of numbers to a common scale.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

As numbers are multiplied and added layer after layer they easily grow or shrink, making later computations (like softmax) extreme and sending the training signal out of control too.

✅ Why this works

Pulling the values back into a common range each time keeps the scale of every layer’s input stable, so a larger learning rate can speed up training without making it collapse.

⚠️ Limits / notes: There are several competing explanations of why normalization works so well, not yet fully settled; its benefits are mainly verified by experiment.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

After all the layers, the next word has to be chosen. The last list of numbers is compared with each word’s “name card” in the vocabulary; the more alike, the higher the score. Then the scores are turned into chances that add up to exactly 100%. Tap the boxes in the picture to see each step.

After all the layers, take the vector at the last position and compare it with each word’s row in the scoring table to get a score for every word; softmax then turns the scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.

👆 Tap a box for details
🤏 Pinch or double-tap100%
Output layerTurns the final vector into “one score for every word in the vocabulary”.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The “what I want to say next” vector has to become “a score for every word in the vocabulary”. The simplest way: give each word a row of numbers and take the dot product of the vector with every row — the more they point the same way, the higher the score. One matrix multiplication scores all words at once.

✅ Why this works

Training pulls the correct word’s row towards the final vector and pulls the vector towards the correct word’s row, so “pointing the same way = this word should come next” is made true by training. See the link below for details.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Dot-product scoring was chosen because it is simple, parallelizes well and has stable gradients — not because it is the only possible design.

Scores (logits)One raw score per candidate word, positive or negative, not yet a probability.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Give “raw scores” first rather than probabilities directly: scores can be positive or negative and are just the result of one multiplication, the easiest thing to compute; “turning them into probabilities” is left to softmax as a separate step.

✅ Why this works

Only the gaps between scores matter (adding the same number to all scores leaves the probabilities unchanged), so the model only has to learn “who is how much higher than whom”. Adjustments like temperature can also act directly on the scores.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

softmax: next-word probabilitiesTurns scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

We need a way to split things up that is “all non-negative and adds up to 100%” while keeping the order of the scores. Raising e to the power guarantees all values are positive; dividing by the total guarantees they add up to 1.

✅ Why this works

Combined with the cross-entropy loss, the gradient is very simple: how much each word’s score should change = predicted probability − correct answer (1 for the correct word, 0 for the others). The more wrong the guess, the stronger the push; a correct guess barely moves; training is very stable.

⚠️ Limits / notes: softmax is a common and effective choice, not the only one.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

At the entrance a table turns each word into a list of numbers; at the exit a table scores each word. The two tables have exactly the same shape but opposite jobs, like one dictionary used once to “look up a meaning” and once to “find a word”. They can share one table to save space, or stay separate for more freedom.

🔍 Go deeper (the full explanation)

Same shape, opposite jobs. By default they are two separate tables, but they can also share one.

Word embedding table (entrance)Output scoring table (exit)
ShapeExactly the same: vocabulary size × vector length (one row per word, thousands of numbers per row)
DirectionID → vector (look up and take one row)Vector → one score per word (dot product with every row)
Question it answers“What does this word mean?”“After what kind of context should this word come next?”
DefaultTwo independent sets of parameters, each trained on its own
🔗 Shared (“weight tying”): the output scoring table is simply the transpose of the embedding table (the same table “used backwards”).
Benefits: ① fewer parameters (saves a whole big “vocabulary × length” table); ② reading in and writing out use the same coordinate system, so a word’s “meaning” and “whether to output it” are naturally aligned. It often works well in small models.
✂️ Separate (untied): the entrance wants “what this word means”, the exit wants “what context this word follows” — not quite the same thing, so separate tables are more flexible. For a large model the extra table is a tiny share of total parameters, so the cost is small and many large models keep them separate.
If they’re separate, the same word has different numbers in the two tables — is that a problem? No. Each table gets its own training signal: the embedding row is adjusted by “what information this word should provide as input”; the scoring row by “which context vectors this word should align with as the answer”. The dozens of layers in between learn to translate between the two “coordinate systems”.
If they are shared, both training signals are added to the same table, which serves both roles at once.

⚠️ Limits / notes: there is no absolute right or wrong in tying vs. not tying; which is better depends on model size and experiments.

③ Hands-on demo

🧒 In plain words first

Why does “comparing how alike they are” pick the right word? At first everything is random and the scores are pure chance. Training makes them right: after each wrong guess, the correct word’s card is pulled a little towards the “current idea”, and the wrong ones are pushed away. After hundreds of millions of rounds, ideas and the words that should follow line up. Drag the sliders below to try (the numbers are an example).

① What is the final vector h? After all the layers, the vector h at the position of “really” condenses “having read the whole sentence, what do I want to say next”.

② What does the dot product measure? Multiply two lists of numbers position by position and add up. The more the two arrows point the same way, the bigger the dot product; pointing opposite ways gives a negative number.

  • ③ This “agreement” means nothing at first — training gives it meaning. At the start h and all rows are random, and high or low dot products are pure coincidence.
  • At each training step the gradient pulls the correct word’s row towards h and at the same time pulls h towards the correct word’s row (h is moved indirectly through the parameters of all earlier layers)
  • wrong words that were overrated are pushed the opposite way.
  • After hundreds of millions of steps, the h for “this kind of context” points the same way as the row of “the word that should follow”.

④ How hard is the push? The gradient of softmax + cross-entropy is remarkably simple: the adjustment to each word’s score = predicted probability − correct answer (1 for the correct word, 0 for the others). If the correct word only got 30%, it’s pushed up by 0.7; if a wrong word got 50%, it’s pushed down by 0.5.

⑤ Why dot product + softmax in particular? It’s simple; one matrix multiplication scores tens of thousands of words at once, which suits GPU parallelism perfectly; gradients are stable and it trains easily. It isn’t the only possible design — just one that is both simple and effective.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

What has the model learned inside? A single neuron often does several jobs at once, so looking at it alone tells you little. Researchers use two kinds of “mind reading”: train a small separate judge to see what information a layer holds, or split a layer into many small features of which only a few light up at a time; those features are far easier to understand than single neurons.

🔍 Go deeper (the full explanation)

Interpretability: probes and features: neurons often do several jobs at once, so we read them another way.

  • Linear probes: take one layer’s activations and train a separate linear classifier (the model is untouched). Deeper layers make features more linearly separable.
  • Sparse autoencoders: split a layer’s activations into many features with only a few active at once. The features are far easier to read than single neurons.

Illustrative The values above are illustrative; the SAE paper does report a feature that fires on apostrophes.

Sources: Alain & Bengio 2016, Linear classifier probes (arXiv 1610.01644) · Cunningham et al. 2023, Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models (arXiv 2309.08600) · Overseas academic / legal site: access from mainland China not tested, and no verified mainland mirror found
